item.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations

Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

By analyzing DNA from the guts of two dragonfly species, the researchers identified a wide range of prey and found dragonflies eat other migrating insects.

The findings reveal a previously hidden "aerial food web," with dragonflies acting as important predators as insects move across landscapes and international borders. The paper, published in the journal Ecography, is titled "Migratory insect flows structure trophic interactions in dragonfly diets."

"We tend to view migrations as a stream of animals moving—but we don't often consider the interactions between them," said Dr. Eva Jimenez-Guri, from the Center for Ecology and Conservation on Exeter's Penryn Campus in Cornwall.

"Our findings show that migration concentrates many species, creating new opportunities for predators and prey to interact."

DNA reveals a varied in-flight diet

Both dragonfly species in the study—the lesser emperor and the common darter—are known to catch prey in flight.

By catching dragonflies at the pass and analyzing their gut contents using a process called DNA metabarcoding, the researchers found:

- Eighty-seven different prey species had been eaten.

- Flies (Diptera) were found in every dragonfly and made up the largest proportion of their diet overall.

- 90% of lesser emperor dragonflies and 70% of darters had eaten species that are known to migrate.

- Crop pest species, including the bean seed fly, were among the species eaten—highlighting the importance of dragonflies for agriculture.

- Some lesser emperors had eaten larger migratory prey, including clouded yellow butterflies.

- The diets of lesser emperors included their smaller dragonfly cousins, the darters.

Dragonflies prey on fellow travelers

"The real surprise for us was that almost all gut samples from lesser emperors contained smaller darter dragonflies," said Dr. Karl Wotton.

"We know that dragonflies prey on each other as nymphs (a juvenile stage when they live in water) but we didn't expect this interaction to appear so consistently in adults traveling along the same route.

"Our results reveal multiple levels of predators and prey traveling together. This is not simply a stream of insects moving south. It is part of a much larger food web moving through the sky."

Publication details

Migratory insect flows structure trophic interactions in dragonfly diets, Ecography (2026). DOI: 10.1002/ecog.09059

Journal information: Ecography

Provided by University of Exeter

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-26 07:30 UTC

item.title: Whitehouse calls on PM to help save lake fish
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Whitehouse calls on PM to help save lake fish

Comedian and TV presenter Paul Whitehouse has called for the government to help save an at-risk fish species present in England's largest lake since the end of the last Ice Age.

Windermere, in the Lake District, has been home to Arctic charr for more than 10,000 years, but campaigners warn extinction beckons as the fish's habitat is harmed by sewage pollution, invasive species competing for food and rising temperatures caused by global warming.

Whitehouse urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to act and said it would be "a crime" if the species were lost.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it shared "the public's determination to protect this iconic lake".

Whitehouse, who fronts the BBC's Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing series alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer, said the "spawning grounds for this beautiful species are covered in algal sludge that is a direct result of sewage pollution".

"This government needs to act now," he added.

The former Fast Show star is helping environmental campaigner Matt Staniek unveil a 1.3m (5ft 6in) ice sculpture depicting the prime minister outside No 10 North, in Manchester, to highlight the fish's plight.

Staniek wants the prime minister to expedite a Â£3.7bn scheme that would include a huge tunnel carrying sewage to a new state-of-the-art water treatment works.

It has been drawn up by the Only Rainwater In Windermere coalition comprising United Utilities (UU), the Environment Agency, Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA), the Love Windermere partnership, Save Windermere campaign group and Westmorland and Furness Council.

It comes as new research from the Freshwater Biological Association (FBA) also warns Arctic charr are in serious decline and face extinction in the lake without "urgent action".

The fish, which is genetically distinct from Arctic charr in the region's other lakes, lives in four separate populations in Windermere that spawn at different times of year and different places and do not interbreed.

The FBA said spawning habitat quality had "declined markedly" at Windermere since 2017 with levels of silt and algae increasing while introduced species, such as ruffe, roach and bream, were "on the rise".

Dr Louise Lavictoire, the organisation's head of science, said the research had "shown very clearly that we are at risk of losing Arctic charr from Windermere completely".

"The species is facing multiple pressures and research gives us the evidence, data and sense of urgency to take collective action to protect this ancient fish species before it's too late."

The research was funded by groups including Natural England, the Environment Agency and the LDNPA.

Natural England's Dave Ottewell described Arctic charr as "remarkable fish" and a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age".

Tim Duckmanton, team leader for strategy and environment at the LDNPA, echoed that sentiment and said "thanks to data collected, we now have a better understanding of threats to the species".

UU, which manages infrastructure around the lake, said protecting the area was a "priority" and that Â£200m was being invested over the next four years in an effort to cut spills from storm overflows and improve wastewater treatment.

A Defra spokesperson said: "This government is already acting to reduce sewage discharges, including deploying 33 additional Environment Agency specialists in the region, increasing inspections and through our regional water council's giving the local community in Windermere a greater say in decision making.

"Our strengthened Water Bill will bring in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

item.title: World's fastest animal could nearly double its livable territory by 2080 in the UK due to climate change
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

World's fastest animal could nearly double its livable territory by 2080 in the UK due to climate change

The area suitable for peregrine falcons within the UK could grow by 74% by the year 2080 under a high-emissions climate scenario, a new study has shown.

This expansion could in principle allow these apex predators to establish more breeding territories. But more suitable area doesn't automatically lead to more birds, warns the author: active conservation and protection interventions are also needed. Furthermore, the picture isn't rosy across the board: habitat for other established species of raptors is on track to decline in the UK unless mitigating measures are taken in time.

"Breeding British birds of prey may respond very differently to future climate change," said Dr. Connor T. Panter, a researcher within the School of Geography at the University of Nottingham and the author of the study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

"Conditions associated with peregrine falcons elsewhere in Europe may become more favorable in the UK under climate change. The area suitable for hen harriers is likewise predicted to expand, while white-tailed eagles and short-eared owls may experience reductions in suitable areas."

Bird's-eye view

Boasting a diversity of raptors is often a hallmark of a healthy, well-balanced ecosystem. By regulating the numbers of small mammals, these species can prevent overgrazing, habitat erosion and the loss of plant biodiversity. Today, five species of owls and 15 species of daytime raptors such as hawks, ospreys and buzzards breed in the UK.

Most suffered devastating declines in the mid-20th century due to the widespread use of organochlorine insecticides, which accumulated in raptors to catastrophic effect.

When the EU banned these compounds from the mid-1970s onward, populations of many raptors tended to bounce back. Nevertheless, the British Trust for Ornithology estimates that the UK's breeding population of peregrine falcons decreased by 57% between 1995 and 2024 due to illegal persecution, declines in available prey and avian flu. Currently, the UK has between 1,750 and 1,800 pairs of peregrines.

Panter aimed to predict changes in environmental suitability across the UK for 16 breeding raptor species under two IPCC emissions scenarios: the "middle-of-the-road" socioeconomic pathway SSP2–4.5 and the "worst-case" SSP5–8.5 pathway. Input for the projections came from "niche models" fitted around 14 environmental variables, including temperature range, various measures of precipitation, elevation and the percentage of land covered by five types of habitat.

Not simply winners versus losers

The results showed that the UK area suitable for peregrine falcons could expand from 110,257 km² (42,600 square miles) today to 155,000 km² (59,800 square miles) (+40.6%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and to 191,319 km² (73,900 square miles) (+73.5%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080.

The area suitable for hen harriers could increase from 74,835 km² (28,900 square miles) today to 96,025 km² (37,100 square miles) (+28.3%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and to 105,553 km² (40,800 square miles) (+41.0%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080. The golden eagle, little owl, long-eared owl, western barn owl and western marsh harrier were likewise predicted to see area increases, albeit by smaller amounts.

The bad news is that the habitat of British short-eared owls, red kites, merlins and Eurasian goshawks is expected to shrink considerably. The white-tailed eagle appears to be worst affected, with suitable habitat potentially disappearing from the UK: namely, a reduction in area from 2,306 km² (890 square miles) today to 444 km² (171 square miles) (-80.7%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and only 65 km² (25 square miles) (-97.2%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080.

In contrast, the area suitable for the common buzzard, European sparrowhawk and tawny owl didn't change by much under any of the models.

Panter concluded that different species are likely to respond in different ways to climate change: the range of outcomes is thus more varied than simply a tally of winners and losers. But what can ordinary people do to help preserve a healthy abundance and diversity of birds of prey in spite of these conflicting trends?

"It is important for everyone to play their part in conserving raptors. This means reducing threats to birds of prey, including shooting and trapping, poisoning, and collisions with human infrastructure such as power lines and wind turbines," said Panter.

"Improving habitat connectivity and preserving existing habitats for both raptors and their prey is equally important. People can also contribute by participating in citizen science programs, such as iNaturalist, where sharing wildlife observations helps scientists better understand and monitor species as their environments change."

Publication details

Contrasting projections of environmental suitability across a breeding raptor assemblage under climate change, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution (2026). DOI: 10.3389/fevo.2026.1922294

Journal information: Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

Provided by Frontiers

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-26 05:00 UTC

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-world-fastest-animal-livable-territory.html

item.title: World’s fastest animal may gain habitat by 2080
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

While climate change represents a threat to most animal populations, the reality isn’t quite as straight forward. As the landscape reacts to a shifting climate, some species might actually see their habitat expand.

That could be the case for peregrine falcons (Falco peregrinus), the fastest animal on the planet, living in the United Kingdom. That’s what Connor Panter, a researcher at the University of Nottingham’s School of Geography, found in a study published today in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

Panter analyzed how various future climate change scenarios might make different parts of the country more or less appropriate for 16 species of breeding birds of prey.

“We know that climate change is altering where wildlife is found across the world, but scientists’ understanding of how different birds of prey may respond to these changes is still relatively limited,” Panter tells Popular Science. “Raptors play important ecological roles as predators, and understanding how their distributions might change is important for informing future conservation efforts.”

Panter investigated a “middle-of-the-road” climate-change scenario and a “worst-case” climate-change scenario in the U.K. Today, there are 42,570 square miles of suitable habitat for peregrine falcons. Under the middle-of-the-road scenario, that could increase by 40.6 percent by 2060, and under the worst-case scenario, it could increase by 73.5 percent by 2080.

Hen harriers (Circus cyaneus), golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos), little owls (Athene noctua), long-eared owls (Asio otus), western barn owls (Tyto alba), and western marsh harriers (Circus aeruginosus) could also see increases. Suitable habitats for common buzzards (Buteo buteo), European sparrowhawks (Accipiter nisus), and tawny owls (Strix aluco), aren’t predicted to change much in any scenario. But British short-eared owls (Asio flammeus), red kites (Milvus milvus), merlins (Falco columbarius), and Eurasian goshawks (Astur gentilis) will likely lose significant amounts of suitable land.

Ultimately, Panter’s work emphasizes that climate change will probably not impact all birds of prey in the same way, even if they live in the same areas. This could represent a significant problem for conservation, because future efforts aiming to safeguard these species will have to take these differences into consideration, according to Panter.

“It is also important to recognise that an increase in the area suitable for a species does not necessarily mean that its population will grow or that it will become more widespread,” Panter says. For example, “whether peregrine falcons can occupy newly suitable areas will depend on numerous other factors, including the availability of prey, nesting opportunities, threats from humans and interactions with other species.”

Source: Popular Science | Published: 2026-11-26 05:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.popsci.com/environment/worlds-fastest-animal-peregeine-falcon-gain-habitat/

item.title: Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?

Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg—who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024—would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut.

To "buy a seat" on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark.

There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a homegrown astronaut to space could benefit industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space.

However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it's costly. As we're in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine, it's crucial to properly analyze some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal.

What counts as an Australian astronaut?

The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately.

The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space. But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn't been given the label of the first "female Australian astronaut."

The federal government hasn't signaled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science Minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal "reckless."

These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then-Science Minister Barry Jones noted it wasn't a high priority. Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in.

The cost would be substantial

We don't know if Australians would support spending $100 million on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut program, but respondents were not given a cost.

Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs, public support decreases. When asked in 2023, more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canceled.

Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently, the Australian Space Agency's funding is $21.7 million over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund the agency for a decade.

Put another way, $100 million is half of the total government investment in space or space-adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occur at universities, in government agencies and in private industry; many organizations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply.

Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There's no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming. An astronaut can't meet all these needs, and we don't know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn't have a whole-of-government space policy, and an astronaut is not a space program.

The suggestion that Australia's growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space?

ESA has a geographic return policy under which member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state and is not looking to become one.

The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it's difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based.

What about inspiration?

Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg's selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country.

However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM.

The selection process was not nationally competitive, and there's no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg's footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space.

We shouldn't ignore the fact that many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it's exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy—after all, we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sports—but we should also recognize that many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space.

Unanswered questions remain

If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are—to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for.

A key final question is: What next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but it also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut.…

Source: Phys.org | Published: 2026-11-26 04:40 UTC

Original link: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-australian-astronaut-space-expensive-worth.html

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

- Date:

November 25, 2026

- Source:

University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science

- Summary:

More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

- Share:

More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

"Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond."

Life thrives in extreme underwater lakes

Brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.

"We were very lucky," said Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project."

Hidden records of ancient tsunamis and earthquakes

Beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

Earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have important implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The study, titled "Discovery of the deep-sea NEOM Brine Pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea," was published on June 27, 2022, in Communications Earth & Environment.

The research team included Sam J. Purkis, Hannah Shernisky, Peter K. Swart, Arash Sharifi, Amanda Oehlert, Gaëlle Duchâtellier, James Klaus, Gregor P. Eberli, Larry Peterson, and Graham Kolodziej from the UM Rosenstiel School; Fabio Marchese and Francesca Benzoni from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Red Sea Research Center; Giovanni Chimienti from the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy; Andrew Craig and Mattie Rodrigue from OceanX; Jürgen Titschack from MARUM -- Center for Marine Environmental Sciences in Germany; and Ameer Abdulla from NEOM.

NEOM, a company developing the Saudi Arabian coastline, provided funding for the four-week research expedition aboard the OceanXplorer.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

- Date:

November 25, 2026

- Source:

Universe Today

- Summary:

A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

- Share:

On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and showed no further changes in brightness.

Researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object

Researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

The third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue

The unusually short duration of the brightening provides an important clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

Phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

To investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

The results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Big Bang.

For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

item.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Worldâs largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

- Date:

November 25, 2026

- Source:

University of Warwick

- Summary:

Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. Despite the advanced technology, patients experienced no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional surgery after one year.

Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

Robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Greater Precision Does Not Improve Recovery

Twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.

The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, said: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an important step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. We are very grateful for the support of the many patients who took part which is so important, but also the NIHR and Stryker for working so well together to support this critical study. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement."

Professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, said: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. These results are by no means a condemnation of the robotic systems, but more understanding of the ideal position for a knee replacement and personalization for each patient is needed. We'll then be able to truly take advantage of the advanced precision of robotic systems."

Professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, said: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. While this study shows robotic-assisted knee replacement is not yet improving patient outcomes, it highlights opportunities to refine these technologies and harness their precision to deliver better care in the future. The NIHR continues to fund robust studies, such as RACER, ensuring we learn how to deliver the latest technologies most effectively within the NHS."

How Robotic Knee Replacement Works

Total knee replacement is among the most frequently performed elective surgical procedures worldwide for people with knee arthritis. During traditional surgery, orthopedic surgeons use standard surgical instruments and rely on their training and experience to position the artificial joint.

Robotic technology offers an alternative approach in which the surgeon controls a robotic arm during the operation. The system helps position surgical instruments with exceptional accuracy and allows surgeons to adjust the angles and depths of their cuts with greater flexibility. These capabilities make it possible to customize procedures to individual anatomy in ways that are not achievable with conventional techniques.

Landmark Trial Finds Similar Patient Outcomes

The study involved 339 patients treated by 33 surgeons at 10 hospitals across the UK.
